messages.subject: Welcome to aroma.affymetrix!
messages.body_plain:
Welcome to aroma.affymetrix!

Aroma.affymetrix is an R package for analyzing large Affymetrix data
sets.  It will allow you to analyze hundreds and most likely thousands
of arrays of various chip types, e.g. expression arrays, SNP chips,
exon arrays, tiling arrays and so on.

In addition to being a forum for aroma.affymetrix users, the intention
is also to collect all available information about the package for
both end users as well as developers on this page, but please do not
forget to look at help pages of the R package distribution.

This package has been under development since January 11, 2006.  Many
changes have been done on the way, but parts of it are now mature
enough for beta testing.  As a first step toward making it public, it
is now available to collaborators.  Please remember that it is an
early beta version.

Henrik Bengtsson
February 1, 2007.

In aroma.affymetrix in general, the design/strategy is such that when
you call a constructor, for instance RmaPlm(), there should be no side
effects to the file system. The call should basically be light-weight,
quick, and return immediately.  In other words, we do not create file
data sets in constructors.

Coupled with any ProbeLevelModel are chip effects and probe
affinities.  We store those to file.  The getChipEffects() and
getProbeAffinities() return those as ChipEffectSet and
ProbeAffinityFile objects.  When calling those the very first time,
there are no files for these, and therefore those two calls creates
*empty* (CEL) files, and provide you with access to those files via
objects of the above two classes.  However, the idea is that you
should not really have to know that the data is on file or in memory.
To avoid having to scan the directories for parameter files and create
a ChipEffectSet for each call to getChipEffects(plm), the
ChipEffectSet object is cached in 'plm' (the ProbeLevelModel object).
Since the ChipEffectSet object does not hold data in memory, this is
cheap.  If you start another R session, there is no ChipEffectSet
object in the cache, so first time you call getChipEffects() that
function will look to the file system, find a set of parameter files
and define a ChipEffectSet object, which is cached in memory, and
available for quick access next time.  To summarize, think about
getChipEffects() as it returns you the chip effects, but it does not
calculate them for you.  You might get calculated data or not, that
depends on if fit() has already been called.  It might even be that
only some of the units (probe sets) have been fitted, e.g. fit(plm,
units=...).  FYI, you can use findUnitsTodo(plm) to find out what
units still haven't been fitted.

Another important thing is that since aroma.affymetrix work towards
files, all data between R sessions is stored in a *shared persistent
memory*, which is a slightly different way of working with data in R.

FYI: I will probably rename the above getChipEffectSet() and
getProbeAffinityFile() to make it more clear what is returned.

> The calculateWeights() function however (called by
> fit.FirmaModel()) seems to require that the residuals are already
> calculated in an earlier step and getResidualSet() is actually linking
> to real data that will be used later. So it seems that
> fit.FirmaModel() requires that the residuals already be calculated

> calculateResiduals() function, not automatically in the fit function?

Support for PLM residuals and weights was added very recently and in a
rush to make FIRMA ready.  Yes, we've been sloppy on the design
pattern here - I knew we would get caught some day but not that fast
;)

I cannot comment on FirmaModel; I'll let Ken do that.

Residuals are slightly different from chip effects and probe
affinities because they are redundant, that is, we can calculate them
give input data, chip effects and probe affinities.  We decided not
store residuals when you fit() a PLM for the reason of saving disk
space.  If residuals are not requested we don't need them, and
whenever/if they are requested we can calculate them.  This is done by
calculateResiduals().  Current that method recalculated *all*
residuals when called twice, but that will be updated to only
calculated them for units not already calculated.

The question is what should happen if you call getResidualSet().
Should it just return the current calculated residuals or should it
always make sure to calculate recently fitted units, or should one
have to call calculateResiduals() first, or should fit() do this
whenever there are residuals on file.  I have to think about this, but
I would appreciate any feedback on this.

About the weights: Ken knows better, but I think the weights are
calculated from the residuals, so yes, those must be available first.
I know we discussed to only store residuals and calculate weights "on
the fly" from those.  I'll let Ken fill in here.

>
>
> And then readUnits() gives a list (by 'unit') of actual intensities
> read from where they are written to file? So if you have
>    rs <- getResidualSet(this, verbose = verbose)
> then rs[i] and readUnits(rs, units=i,...) gives the same thing?

First, the name getUnits() is "trademarked" by BioC so we had to use
another name, and readUnits() was the best one.  However, you should
think of it as getUnits(), i.e. a function that you can use to get
data structured unit by unit as a list.

Second, yes rs[i] equals readUnits(rs, units=i), and was added just
for convenience.  The first calls the second, but that is also the
only overhead, so you should consider these to be equally fast.
However, readUnits() provides more alternatives that would not be
possible to do with a "[" subsetting call.  Thumb of rule: If you just
work on at the R prompt or simple scripts, rs[i] is fine to use, but
if you add new methods/classes, it is recommended to use readUnits()
to make the code more explicit about what is going on.

Hope this helps, and thanks for all your constructive feedback.

Cheers

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] residual calculation
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

see Section "Quality assessment of summarized data" on the group page;
how the residuals are calculated depends on what PLM you used.  Yes,
for the log-additive model it is on the log scale.

In the code, this is taken care of by the
getCalculateResidualsFunction() method.  The default implementation
for any ProbeLevelModel is to calculate the residuals as the
difference on the intensity scale, but subclasses such as RmaPlm
provide alternative implementations, e.g.
getCalculateResidualsFunction.RmaPlm().  The latter, as you found out,
calculates this as:

 e = y/yhat

The rational for this is that 'e' is on the intensity scale, which
will give you:

 log2(e) = log(y) - log(yhat)

as you expected.  (Footnote: As all signals in aroma.affymetrix,
residuals, are always store on the intensity scale, because it more
generic than the log scale which is only defined for (0,Inf)).

In the group pages under "For Developers", there is a section on
reproducibility with a graph showing that the above calculations give
close to identical results as what you affyPLM() returns.

Cheers

Henrik

messages.subject: aroma.affymetrix v0.4.1 released
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

it is good to hear that people are getting their analysis going now
using aroma.affymetrix on both Unix and Windows.  There's been a some
initial hiccups for people who get started with the package for the
first time.  Since me and Ken are already up and running we might miss
such problems when we update the package, although we once in a while
try to test it all from scratch.

Your feedback has been good and we've been modifying the code
accordingly.  A new version is now available, which hopefully solves
most of those problems.  A new required version of affxparser (v1.7.4)
is now also available.  Just follow the installations/updates
instructions on "Download & Install" page at:

  http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/

and you should get a better working package in a few minutes.

Finally, please use this forum for questions and feedback by sending
an email to aroma-af...@googlegroups.com.  By sharing problems
and questions hopefully everyone learn something and it also saves us
some time.  If anyone wants to, we can give you permission to update
the help pages or write your own, e.g. example scripts etc. That would
be just great.

Cheers

Henrik

PS. If you wonder why you receive this, I manually activated the email
messages for all group members. To change your settings to something,
see the group page. DS.

columns: x, y, intensities, stdvs, pixels.  Extracting x or y seems redundant

the number of rows and columns, which is in the CDF), but I guess they might

messages.body_plain:
Hi.

Maybe it is the NSI ;)  Seriously, sorry that you had problems with
this.  It is the R.utils package that modifies you .Last() such that
it first calls finalizeSession() and the calls your original .Last(),
which has been renamed to .LastOriginal().  See below for more
details.  So, yes, you're right, it is unrelated to aroma.affymetrix.

I'm trying to figure out what is happening because I haven't heard of
this before.  One likely scenario could be that you load R.utils, then
store your session (.RData), and then when you start R without loading
R.utils and tries to exit the patched .Last() from the "R.utils"
session is called and you get an error that finalizeSession() cannot
be found.  It sounds from you description that this is actually the
case.  Note that R.utils do not modify any files or similar, so you
should only see this when you load R.utils.

I will update the "patch" so that 1) it never stops with an error by
using a tryCatch() call, and 2) call R.utils::finalizeSession()
explicitly so that the package does not have to be loaded.

Before that is updated, the quick fix is to do:

 .Last <- .LastOriginal

If there is not .LastOriginal, then just do rm(.Last).

Details below.

Sorry about the mess. Thanks for telling me.

Henrik

DETAILS:

The finalizeSession() method defined in R.utils calls "onSessionExit"
hooks (functions).  If no hooks are set, nothing extra is done.  The
reason for doing all this is to add a general way for packages and
other code to always be called when R exits.  I added this in June
2005, and at the same time I asked if there was a similar feature
already in R, but there wasn't, cf.
http://tolstoy.newcastle.edu.au/R/devel/05/06/1206.html.  Example of
the modification follows.

% R
> .Last
function() {
  if (interactive()) savehistory();
}
> library(R.utils)
Loading required package: R.oo
R.oo v1.2.5 (2006-01-05) successfully loaded. See ?R.oo for help.
R.utils v0.8.3 (2006-11-10) successfully loaded. See ?R.utils for help.
> .Last
function (...)
{
    finalizeSession()
    if (exists(".LastOriginal", mode = "function"))
        .LastOriginal()
}
<environment: 0x02678824>
attr(,"finalizeSession")
[1] TRUE
> .LastOriginal
function() {
  if (interactive()) savehistory();
}

STOP. /HB

What does getCdf(csN) on the CEL set in between give?  This will help
me troubleshoot.

BTW/FYI, the QuantileNormalizer keeps the chip type of the input CEL
files and do not update it to the chip type of the CDF set by
setCdf(cs, cdf).  This is due to the way QN is implemented (copying
source CEL file and then update its data; the chip type is in the CEL
header and that does not get updated), and not due to an explicit
design strategy. I never though about changing the CDF before the QN
but only directly before the PLM, so I did not think of this scenario.
 It should only make a difference to the QN if QN is done on PMs or
MMs only and if these are different in the new CDF.  I will put it on
the to do list of updates, but it is not on the urgent list since in
most case it is sufficient to do setCdf(csN, cdf).

A possible reason for your problem (the bug?) may be that the core CDF
is carried through when the analysis is done the first time, but if
restarted and parts are already fitted, this somehow fails.  If so, it
is a bug and will be fixed.

>

logFile <- sprintf("%s.log", dataSetName);
log <- Verbose(logFile, threshold=-4, removeFile=FALSE);

and pass this to your method calls via argument 'verbose', e.g.

mechanism that always log to file, but other things are more
prioritized.)

Ok, this explains it.  I've now fixed it so that both
getOutputDataSet() and process() is guaranteed to carry down the same
AffymetrixCdfFile object as set in the input data set.  This will be
available in the next version.  In the meantime, do the same manually:

setCdf(csN, getCdf(cs))

Details: When process() is called and the data has not yet been
normalized, the code that does the normalization (the function Ken
refers to above) does also make sure that the CDF is carried down.
When process() is called on data already normalized, that code is not
called, but instead just getOutputDataSet().  The getOutputDataSet()
method is where the problem was; it did not pass down the CDF.  So,
the fix was simple.  BTW, since getOutputDataSet() is define in
superclass Transform, this fix should apply to all transformation
(calibration, normalization, ...) methods inheriting from Transform.

Cheers

Henrik
